https://www.thenews.com.pk/latest/141016.text: Sarah Ferguson’s charity removed from official register after closure Sarah Ferguson’s charity officially shuts down after Epstein controversy Sarah’s Trust has officially closed months after renewed attention on Sarah Ferguson's past links to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. The charity announced in February that it would shut down "for the foreseeable future." At the time, the board said the decision had been under discussion for several months and praised the charity’s work. Sarah’s Trust has now been removed from the public charity register. The charity was launched in 2020 during the COVID-19 pandemic. It supported NHS workers, care home staff and hospices, and also helped provide computers for Ukrainian refugees in Poland. The closure announcement came days after the US Department of Justice released millions of documents related to Epstein. Some emails showed Ferguson was in contact with him after he was released from prison in 2009 for soliciting prostitution from a minor. One email from Epstein to Ghislaine Maxwell said Ferguson and her daughters, Princess Beatrice and Princess Eugenie, had visited him shortly after his release. Other emails showed Ferguson thanking Epstein for his support. In one message, she called him "the brother I have always wished for." In another, she said she needed £20,000 to cover rent after one of her business ventures failed. The documents also included emails in which Ferguson discussed possible business opportunities with Epstein. Being named in the documents does not mean Ferguson committed any wrongdoing. Ferguson divorced Prince Andrew in 1996. Andrew later stepped back from royal duties and stopped using his Duke of York title following his own links to Epstein. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c790.text: Image source, EPA Image caption, The remains of Genghis Khan, an 11-year-old bull elephant, lay near the outskirts of Amboseli National Park By Emily Atkinson Â and Â Thomas Mukhwana ,Â BBC Africa Published 1 hour ago Four people have been arrested in Kenya as part of an investigation into a spate of mysterious elephant deaths over the past two months, officials have said. Three Kenyans and one Tanzanian have been detained on suspicion of poisoning at least 18 elephants in the Amboseli National Park, the Kenya Wildlife Service told the BBC. The investigation is looking into whether the elephants died from cyanide poisoning after eating large quantities of tomatoes sprayed with illegal pesticides. Preliminary laboratory tests have found traces of cyanide in samples of the crops taken from the elephants' stomachs. All of the affected elephants - mainly female adults and their calves - had also shown signs of paralysis, which authorities believe also points to cyanide poisoning. Tomato farms are found in the Kimana area, which is part of a corridor between Amboseli National Park and the Tsavo National Park in southern Kenya. It is a vast area known as the Amboseli ecosystem, which straddles the border near Tanzania where more than 2,000 elephants move along in search of food and water. Pesticides prohibited in Kenya are sometimes smuggled across this porous border with Tanzania and used in farms within the Amboseli area, where elephants live near human settlements and are known to raid farms for food. While regulations against illegal agrochemicals exist, there is weak enforcement and little attention paid to how they can affect animals. The suspects have been released on bail and the investigation continues. https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/se.text: Catherine Corless and Liam Neeson at the Dublin gala screening of The Lost Children of Tuam. Photograph: GEMC/GMD/Backgrid View image in fullscreen Catherine Corless and Liam Neeson at the Dublin gala screening of The Lost Children of Tuam. Photograph: GEMC/GMD/Backgrid Movies ‘She never accepted no’: Liam Neeson on dogged heroine behind Tuam mass baby grave film Catherine Corless’s exposure of almost 800 infant deaths at a home led by nuns prompted Neeson to bring the story to screen Rory Carroll Ireland correspondent Fri 25 Sep 2026 05.53 EDT First published on Fri 25 Sep 2026 02.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Liam Neeson still remembers his shock and shame when he read a New York Times article about the mother and baby institution in Tuam, County Galway. It was 2017 and the article chronicled the campaign by Catherine Corless , an amateur local historian, to expose abuse and neglect by Irish nuns that led to hundreds of children being buried in a mass, unmarked grave. “I had such a visceral reaction,” Neeson told the Guardian. “I’m obviously Irish, I was raised in the Catholic church, and I had a deep sense of embarrassment and obligation for the truth to come out and for there to be some accountability.” View image in fullscreen Liam Neeson, the producer of The Lost Children of Tuam, says he felt a deep sense of obligation to expose the truth. Photograph: Gareth Cattermole/Getty for IMDb It prompted the actor – and former altar boy – to use his heft in the film industry to become a producer for the first time. He optioned the article, visited Corless at her home and assembled a team to put the story on screen. The result, nine years later, is The Lost Children of Tuam, a feature film that is released in Ireland this week and in the UK next month. “This was such an important story for the world to know about and to give a voice to the hundreds of babies and children that died,” said Neeson. The release coincides with the continuing excavation of a 5,000 sq metre (53,820 sq ft) site where the Bon Secours order is believed have interred 796 infants who died at the St Mary’s mother and baby home between 1925 and 1961. View image in fullscreen Catherine Corless at the site of the former mother and baby home in Tuam, County Galway, where it is believed 796 infants were buried. Photograph: Rory Carroll/The Guardian An international team of forensic archaeologists and other specialists has found skeletal remains of 99 babies and children since starting work last year – the result of Corless’s research, a judicial commission and a promise by the Irish state to seek truth and justice for survivors and relatives of those who died. It is part of a wider reckoning of the mistreatment of women and children in state- and religious-run institutions across Ireland . Tuam, however, stands out for its macabre details – some infants were buried in a disused subterranean septic tank – and the doggedness of the woman who exposed it. View image in fullscreen Monica Dolan, who plays Catherine Corless, in a scene from The Lost Children of Tuam. Photograph: Element Pictures In her quest for answers, Corless never accepted “no”, said Neeson. “The detective work she did to uncover this atrocity involving the relationship between the state and the church was extraordinary.” The film, based on the New York Times article by Dan Barry , tells the story of how Corless, a former textile factory secretary with an interest in local history, began researching the site for an essay. Officials and the Bon Secours order fobbed her off but Corless discovered that 796 children had died without burial records before the institution was closed in 1961 and demolished. Early reviews of the film, which was written by Rebecca Lenkiewicz and directed by Frank Berry , say it is sensitive and stirring, with the English actor Monica Dolan giving a powerful central performance. View image in fullscreen Director Frank Berry, Monica Dolan and Liam Neeson promote The Lost Children of Tuam in Toronto. Photograph: Gareth Cattermole/Getty for IMDb “She’s brilliant – so natural, so down to earth,” said Corless. “She portrayed me as I am. She has an English accent so how on earth did she capture the way I speak?” Andrew Bennett, who plays her husband, Aidan, has also captured his personality and the couple’s relationship, she said. Corless has watched the film three times – two private viewings for her family and survivors, and the premiere at the Galway film Fleadh in July, where it won best Irish film. “I was so nervous I needed to see it a few times,” she said. View image in fullscreen Andrew Bennett and Monica Dolan, who play Aidan and Catherine Corless, captured the couple’s personality and relationship, says Corless. Photograph: Element Pictures “We’re ordinary people. We have a farm. That a film would be made about us, it was out of this world. It’s done with great respect, with the odd little bit of humour in it too, and it just hits people, it hits you hard.” Berry, the director , said the film showed Corless’s integrity and persistence. “Her work revealed a lot of very hard truths about Ireland. It’s a way of telling truths but with an inspirational central character. It shows that one person can achieve amazing things.” Explore more on these topics Film Ireland Liam Neeson Children Catholicism Religion Christianity features Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story ‘I’m so grateful I got to live these days’: A Ghost in the Throat author Doireann Ní Ghríofa on recovering from depression ‘I see the incredible promise’: on set of an AI film shoot as new studios embrace controversial tech The Fallen by Louise Brangan review – an enraging account of Ireland’s Magdalene laundries ‘Bored by all the sex and violins’: readers on Wuthering Heights film Meet the unlikely star of the bodice-ripping Wuthering Heights: Martin Clunes Survivors of Ireland’s mother and baby homes will not have UK benefits cut Testimony review – a devastating exposé of the Irish church’s brutal Magdalene laundries ‘Begging my boyfriend to get one’: Paul Mescal inspires yet another fashion craze with Hamnet earring Dig begins at site in Ireland believed to hold remains of nearly 800 infants Going nuclear: Kathryn Bigelow back in geopolitical territory with atomic thriller Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

https://www.baltictimes.com/un_block_fin.text: Estonia Latvia Lithuania Business Analysis Opinions Culture EU Affairs Search Archive UN:BLOCK Fintech to Bring Together More Than 600 Fintech Professionals in Riga to Discuss Licensing, Cross-Border Payments and Capital Mobilisation 2026-10-05 On October 15, more than 600 fintech professionals, private investors and European Union regulators will gather in Riga for UN:BLOCK Fintech, a one-day conference exploring the issues reshaping financial services. Key topics will include MiCA regulation, cross-border payments, capital mobilisation, artificial intelligence, financial literacy, and partnerships between banks and fintech companies. One of the conference’s key discussions will focus on Latvia’s underutilised capital, with approximately €9 billion held in savings and pension assets. In the session “Who Wakes Up Latvia’s €9 Billion Dormant Capital?”, industry representatives will explore how to channel more of this capital into investment and economic development. Panellists will include Dana Gorina (Digilo), Nauris Bloks (Twino), Mārtiņš Valters (Mintos) and Māra Meiere (AS Crefo Birojs). MiCA regulation and its impact on the crypto-asset sector will also feature prominently. In the session “5 CEOs Behind Latvia’s First MiCA Licences”, company leaders will share their experiences with the licensing process and discuss what it means for business growth across the European Union. Panellists will include Can Sun (Backpack EU), Alex Novozhenov (Nodu), Sławek Zawadzki (Kanga Exchange) and Vytautas Zabulis (H Finance). A separate discussion on cross-border payments will bring together representatives from Bolt, Paybis, Nexpay, SEB and Latvijas Banka to examine why international payments can still be slow and costly. The programme will also feature discussions on the development of the Baltic fintech ecosystem, partnerships between banks and businesses, financial literacy and the future of payments. Practical workshops will cover MiCA, licensing for payment and electronic money institutions, crowdfunding and AML requirements. Participants will also have the opportunity to meet with experts from Latvijas Banka and other industry organisations. Latvia is emerging as a launchpad for fintech and crypto companies looking to build and scale across Europe. A growing ecosystem, forward-looking regulation and a crypto-friendly business environment make the country an increasingly attractive base for EU-wide businesses. Latvia is also among the pioneers in creating practical ways for companies to work with digital assets, including allowing company share capital to be paid in crypto, with further digital-asset initiatives on the way. “Northern Europe’s fintech scene continues to grow, attracting increasing interest from businesses and retail investors alike. We believe the UN:BLOCK Fintech Forum will create valuable opportunities for business development, while giving private investors the chance to explore emerging sectors, innovative financial products, and compelling new investment opportunities,” says Reinis Znotiņš, Executive Director of The Latvian Blockchain Association. UN:BLOCK Fintech will bring together more than 600 founders, regulators, investors and experts shaping the future of financial technology. Participants will include representatives from companies such as Bolt, SEB, Citadele, Twino, Paybis, Backpack EU, NBX and other leading industry players. Conference partners include the Investment and Development Agency of Latvia (LIAA), Magnetiq Bank, Digilo, Nexpay, Mastercard, Bolt, Mintos and Tribe Payments. The UN:BLOCK Fintech programme will feature panel discussions, expert presentations and thematic workshops. This format will give participants the opportunity to stay up to date with the latest industry developments, explore topics in greater depth and build new professional connections. The conference is designed to offer practical value to every participant – from early-stage startup founders to leaders of established companies. UN:BLOCK Fintech is a new one-day conference from the team behind Northern Europe's leading annual blockchain and fintech conference UN:BLOCK Europe, taking place in Riga on March 10-11, 2027. The conference is organized in cooperation with the Latvian Blockchain Association. Support is provided within the framework of the project “Support for the Improvement of the Technology Transfer System”, co-financed by the European Regional Development Fund and the Latvian state budget.
